questions.question_markdown: A diagnostic test is 99% sensitive and 99% specific for a disease with prevalence 1% in the population. Given a positive test result, what is the probability that the person actually has the disease?
questions.explanation_markdown: By Bayes' theorem: P(D|+) = (0.99 x 0.01) / (0.99 x 0.01 + 0.01 x 0.99) = 0.0099 / 0.0198 = 0.5. Base-rate matters: even a very accurate test gives only 50% posterior for a rare disease.

questions.question_markdown: If events A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4, what is P(A n B)?
questions.explanation_markdown: For independent events, P(A n B) = P(A) x P(B) = 0.5 x 0.4 = 0.20.

questions.question_markdown: For an m x n matrix A, the rank-nullity theorem states that rank(A) + nullity(A) equals:
questions.explanation_markdown: rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of columns (dimension of the domain).

questions.question_markdown: PCA finds the directions (principal components) that:
options: minimize the variance of the projected data
maximize the variance of the projected data
minimize the number of original features
questions.explanation_markdown: PCA is unsupervised and picks orthogonal directions maximizing projected variance (equivalently, minimizing reconstruction error) - the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

questions.question_markdown: A model with low bias but high variance is most likely:
questions.explanation_markdown: High variance (sensitive to training data) with low bias is the classic signature of overfitting.

questions.question_markdown: In k-Nearest Neighbours, increasing the value of k generally:
options: makes the decision boundary smoother (higher bias, lower variance)
has no effect on the decision boundary
questions.explanation_markdown: Larger k averages over more neighbours, smoothing the decision boundary - raising bias and lowering variance. Too large a k underfits.

questions.question_markdown: The worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements is:
questions.explanation_markdown: Binary search halves the search space each step, giving O(log n) worst-case comparisons.

questions.topic_name: Divide-and-conquer sorting (merge sort, quick sort - including stability and worst/average case)
questions.question_markdown: The worst-case time complexity of quicksort is:
questions.explanation_markdown: With poor pivots (e.g. already-sorted input with a naive pivot), quicksort degrades to O(n^2). Its average case is O(n log n).

questions.topic_name: Divide-and-conquer sorting (merge sort, quick sort - including stability and worst/average case)
questions.question_markdown: Which of the following comparison-based sorting algorithms have O(n log n) worst-case time complexity? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation_markdown: Merge sort and heapsort are O(n log n) worst-case. Quicksort is O(n^2) worst-case; bubble sort is O(n^2).
